options.reflection: Local, right-sized models trade polish for control. When processing stays on site, you know where the data is, how long it lives, and how much energy it consumes — three things a humanitarian organisation should always be able to answer.

options.label: No AI — fund admin volunteers instead
options.detail: Recruit volunteer medical secretaries to type notes after each shift.
options.consequence: Recruitment works in your city's student community, and patients notice no change. But secretaries are hard to keep through the exam season, and in the evening clinic doctors are back to typing until midnight.
options.reflection: Saying no to AI is a legitimate choice with real costs, often carried by exhausted staff and volunteers. The question is not whether AI is good or bad, but whether a lighter alternative serves people better here.

steps.title: Consent in the waiting room
steps.narrative: Whatever tool you use, patients must be told they are being recorded. Your team drafts a consent form. One volunteer suggests a simple checkbox at registration. An interpreter warns that many patients will tick anything a person in a Red Cross vest hands them, out of fear of being turned away.

options.label: A checkbox at registration
options.detail: Quick and legally tidy. Patients agree once for all future visits.
options.consequence: Consent rates are 99%. An audit later finds that most patients did not understand what they agreed to — several believed it was a condition of treatment.
options.reflection: Consent given under dependency is not free consent. When people need help, a checkbox measures compliance, not understanding.

options.label: Ask at every visit, with a real 'no'
options.detail: The clinician asks in the patient's language at the start of each consultation. Saying no changes nothing about the care.
options.consequence: About one in five patients says no, mostly the newest arrivals. Their notes are typed by hand. Trust grows: patients tell others that the clinic asks, and means it.
options.reflection: An opt-out that carries no penalty is what makes AI support acceptable. Keeping a non-AI path open protects the people who most need it.

options.label: Record only the clinician's summary
options.detail: No patient voice is recorded. After the consultation, the clinician dictates a short summary into the tool.
options.consequence: The patient's words never touch the machine. Time savings are smaller, but dictation is quick, the audio is tiny, and processing needs a fraction of the energy of full-conversation transcription.
options.reflection: Data minimisation can be a design choice: change what you capture rather than protecting what you shouldn't have captured. Less data is also less computing, storage and energy.

steps.title: The hidden bill
steps.narrative: The regional Red Cross branch wants to roll transcription out to all twelve health and psychosocial support points in western Sweden — and to keep every recording for five years 'to train a better model later'. Your IT volunteer does the maths: storing and repeatedly reprocessing thousands of hours of audio would need a server room's worth of electricity and cooling every year.

options.label: Keep everything for future training
options.detail: More data might mean better models. Storage is cheap, and Sweden's grid is mostly fossil-free.
options.consequence: The archive grows to terabytes of the most sensitive conversations your organisation has ever held. Energy use climbs every month. Nobody ever trains the model, but the archive must still be secured, backed up and powered.
options.reflection: A clean grid does not make waste harmless: electricity used here is electricity not available for other needs, and hardware has a heavy footprint before it is ever switched on. Data kept 'just in case' carries privacy risk and energy cost indefinitely.

options.label: Delete audio, measure and publish energy use
options.detail: Audio deleted within 24 hours. Each site reports energy per consultation, and the numbers go in the annual report.
options.consequence: The first figures surprise everyone: the cloud pilot used about thirty times more energy per note than the local model. The board adopts an energy budget per consultation, and two branches choose the local model on that basis.
options.reflection: You cannot manage a footprint you refuse to measure. Publishing the energy cost of AI turns sustainability from a slogan into a decision rule communities and donors can check.

options.label: Roll out only where volunteers ask for it
options.detail: No region-wide mandate. Sites opt in after reviewing the evidence from your clinic.
options.consequence: Five sites adopt it, seven don't. Usage — and energy — stays proportionate to real need, but practices differ and the data protection officer now has five configurations to check.
options.reflection: Scaling should follow evidence of value, not enthusiasm. Smaller footprints often come from simply not deploying where a tool isn't needed.

steps.title: When the note is wrong
steps.narrative: A patient returns with a worsening infection. The AI-drafted note from her first visit said 'no known allergies'. She had said, through the interpreter, that she was allergic to penicillin. The volunteer doctor approved the note at the end of a twelve-hour shift without reading it closely.

options.label: Treat it as individual human error
options.detail: Remind the doctor to read more carefully. Keep the workflow as is.
options.consequence: Two months later, a different volunteer approves a different wrong note. The pattern is the same: tired people, long shifts, notes that look confident.
options.reflection: Automation bias is predictable: polished text invites approval. Blaming individuals hides a design problem that will repeat.

options.label: Make critical fields human-only
options.detail: Allergies, medication and safety risks are always asked and typed by the clinician. The AI drafts only the narrative.
options.consequence: Notes take a little longer, and errors on critical fields drop to zero in the next audit. You tell the patient what happened, apologise, and explain the change — she agrees to keep coming.
options.reflection: Meaningful human oversight means designing where humans decide, not just asking them to sign. Being open with the person affected is part of accountability.

options.label: Pause AI and review with patients
options.detail: Stop transcription for a month and invite former patients and interpreters to review how it should work.
options.consequence: The pause costs volunteer hours. The review produces the clinic's best idea yet: interpreters read the key facts back to patients before the note is approved. It's slower, and errors become rare.
options.reflection: Those affected by a system are often best placed to see where it fails. Pausing to listen is not failure — it is how humanitarian accountability works in practice.

title: The Invoice Engine
tagline: Automating finance admin at a national office in the Netherlands
role: Director of Finance & Administration, National Society headquarters in The Hague
context: Your finance team processes 40,000 invoices a year: suppliers for shelters, refunds to volunteers, payments to partner organisations abroad, and cash transfers to people affected by the floods in Limburg. Three of your eight staff are retiring. A large software vendor offers an AI agent that reads invoices, codes them, flags fraud and approves routine payments automatically. The board wants savings that can go to programmes.
debrief: The Invoice Engine shows that back-office AI shapes who gets paid, who gets flagged and how much energy the organisation burns doing it. Efficiency is a legitimate humanitarian goal — but only when people stay accountable for payments, flags can be challenged, and the lightest tool that works is chosen over the most impressive one.

steps.title: Which tool for the job?
steps.narrative: The vendor's agent runs every invoice through a large general-purpose AI model in the cloud — even the simple ones that follow the same template each month. Your controller notes that 80% of your invoices come from just 200 regular suppliers. An ICT volunteer suggests that ordinary rule-based automation, plus a small model for the messy remainder, would do most of the work.

options.label: Buy the full AI agent
options.detail: One platform for everything. Every invoice, simple or complex, goes through a large model.
options.consequence: It works, impressively. It also costs more than the staff it replaces, and its usage report reveals that each simple recurring invoice uses as much computing as a long chat conversation — tens of thousands of times a year.
options.reflection: Using a large AI model for a task a simple rule can do is like sending a lorry to deliver a letter. Every unnecessary query carries an energy, water and hardware cost.

options.label: Rules first, small AI for the rest
options.detail: Plain automation for recurring invoices; a small model reads only the unusual ones; staff handle exceptions.
options.consequence: It takes three months to build with your ICT team. Recurring invoices fly through with almost no computing. The small model handles handwritten receipts from volunteers. Running costs and energy use are a fraction of the vendor offer.
options.reflection: Frugal design is a principle, not a compromise: start with the simplest tool and add AI only where it adds clear value. That is also how you keep the system understandable to auditors.

options.label: Hire and train instead
options.detail: Replace the retiring staff with two new hires and improve the existing system.
options.consequence: Payments stay accurate and people stay accountable. But recruitment takes months, backlogs reach six weeks, and some small suppliers in flood areas wait too long to be paid.
options.reflection: Not automating is a legitimate choice — but late payment is also a harm, especially to small local businesses and volunteers who advance their own money.

steps.title: The fraud flag
steps.narrative: The automated checks begin flagging 'high-risk' payments. You notice a pattern: refunds to volunteers with non-Dutch names and transfers to partner organisations in Syria and Sudan are flagged three times more often. Each flag freezes the payment for up to three weeks.

options.label: Trust the flags — risk comes first
options.detail: Compliance is non-negotiable. Frozen payments are the price of safety.
options.consequence: Two partner organisations in Sudan miss payroll. A volunteer of Eritrean origin who paid for blankets with her own money waits a month for a refund and quits. The flags catch no actual fraud.
options.reflection: A model trained on past patterns reproduces past suspicion. Applied to names and destinations, it turns into discrimination — against the very people and partners a humanitarian organisation exists to serve.

options.label: Audit the flags for bias
options.detail: Pause automatic freezes, test the flags against outcomes, and remove names and nationality as signals.
options.consequence: The audit shows the flags were mostly picking up names and geography, not risk. After the changes, flag rates are even across groups, and the two genuine fraud cases of the year are still caught — by a human investigator following up on a tip.
options.reflection: Impartiality applies to back-office systems too. Testing automated decisions for unequal outcomes is a duty, not a nice-to-have.

options.label: Flags only advise; humans decide within 48 hours
options.detail: No automatic freezes. A finance officer reviews each flag and must decide within two days.
options.consequence: The team grumbles about the extra workload, but frozen payments drop to almost zero. The officers also start writing down why they clear flags, which becomes useful evidence for improving the rules.
options.reflection: Keeping humans in the decision — with a deadline that protects the person waiting — balances control with dignity.

steps.title: Where does the computing happen?
steps.narrative: The vendor plans to move all processing to a new data centre in the north of the Netherlands — the same region where local residents have protested about data centres taking land, electricity and water. A local journalist asks whether the Red Cross is part of the problem.

options.label: Leave it to the vendor
options.detail: Where the vendor computes is the vendor's business. Their sustainability report says 'carbon neutral'.
options.consequence: The journalist's article quotes your silence. When you ask the vendor for numbers, 'carbon neutral' turns out to rely on offsets bought elsewhere; the actual water and electricity use is not published.
options.reflection: Responsibility does not end at the contract. Ethical procurement includes asking where computing happens and what it costs the local community and environment.

options.label: Make energy reporting a contract term
options.detail: Require the vendor to report energy, water and location per year, with a right to exit if targets aren't met.
options.consequence: Negotiations take two extra months. The vendor agrees, partly because other NGOs follow your lead. You publish the first report — the numbers are modest because of your rules-first design.
options.reflection: Procurement is power. When humanitarian organisations ask together, vendors begin to disclose what they otherwise hide.

options.label: Run the small model on your own servers
options.detail: Host the invoice model in your existing server room, powered by your rooftop solar and green contract.
options.consequence: Your ICT team now maintains one more system, and performance dips during the year-end peak. But you know exactly what the system uses — and it is less than the office coffee machines.
options.reflection: Owning the infrastructure brings responsibility as well as control. For small, steady workloads, local hosting can be both more independent and lighter.

steps.title: Who signs?
steps.narrative: The system now works well. The board proposes the final step: let it approve and pay all invoices under €5,000 automatically — including the small cash transfers to flood-affected households in Limburg. No human would see them.

options.label: Full automation under €5,000
options.detail: Maximum efficiency. Exceptions are investigated afterwards.
options.consequence: A data error in a list import sends double payments to 300 households, then automatically claws them back a week later. Families who had already spent the money on repairs receive debt letters. The headlines are not about efficiency.
options.reflection: When automated payments touch people affected by a crisis, errors become harm at scale. Small amounts are not small to the people who receive them.

options.label: Automate suppliers, keep humans on people
options.detail: Routine supplier invoices go through automatically. Payments to individuals always have a human sign-off.
options.consequence: Most of the volume is automated; the payments that touch people's lives still have a name attached. When the import error happens, a finance officer catches it before a single double payment leaves.
options.reflection: Draw the line for automation where errors stop being administrative and start being personal.

options.label: Automate, but publish how to appeal
options.detail: Automation under €5,000, with a clear phone line and a 5-day promise to fix any wrong payment.
options.consequence: The appeal line catches problems fast, and most are fixed within days. But it puts the burden on people affected to notice and complain — and those with the least time and language skills complain least.
options.reflection: An appeal route is essential, but it is not a substitute for preventing harm. Accountability works best before the error, not only after it.

title: The Volunteer Roster
tagline: AI scheduling for refugee-reception volunteers in Poland
role: Volunteer Coordinator, Red Cross branch in Kraków
context: Two years after the first wave of arrivals from Ukraine, your branch still runs reception, language cafés and a food distribution point. You coordinate 1,800 volunteers through spreadsheets, WhatsApp groups and a lot of late-night phone calls. Shifts go uncovered and the same reliable people are asked again and again. A Polish tech company offers an AI system that predicts demand, builds the roster and messages volunteers automatically.
debrief: The Volunteer Roster shows that an AI that optimises people's time is also making decisions about people — who is trusted, who is overlooked, who is pushed too hard. Volunteers are not resources to be maximised. The right system protects their wellbeing, collects as little about them as possible, and uses no more computing than the problem needs.

steps.title: What the system wants to know
steps.narrative: To predict who will turn up, the vendor wants to connect to volunteers' phone location data, social media activity and calendars, and to score each person's 'reliability'. The demo is impressive: it predicts no-shows with 85% accuracy.

options.label: Connect everything — accuracy matters
options.detail: The more data, the better the roster.
options.consequence: The predictions are accurate. Then volunteers find out. Several Ukrainian volunteers, refugees themselves, leave immediately — they fled a war where phone tracking meant danger. Others feel watched in their free time.
options.reflection: Volunteers are people, not data sources. Tracking their lives beyond the role breaks trust and can endanger those with their own protection concerns.

options.label: Only what volunteers choose to share
options.detail: Availability they enter themselves, their skills and languages. No tracking, no reliability scores.
options.consequence: Predictions are less precise. But volunteers trust the system and keep their availability up to date — which turns out to matter more than any tracking signal.
options.reflection: Data minimisation is respect in practice. Information people give willingly is often more reliable than information taken from them.

options.label: A shared calendar, no AI
options.detail: A simple open-source scheduling tool. Volunteers pick their own shifts.
options.consequence: It costs almost nothing to run and uses barely any energy. Popular shifts fill instantly; the early-morning food distribution still goes uncovered, and you are still making the 6 a.m. calls.
options.reflection: Simple tools are often enough — but it's worth asking which problems they leave unsolved, and for whom.

steps.title: The optimised roster
steps.narrative: The scheduling system learns that a small group of volunteers almost always says yes. It starts giving them most of the hard shifts. One of them — a retired teacher who has volunteered every week for two years — tells you she can't sleep anymore.

options.label: Keep optimising for coverage
options.detail: Full coverage is what people arriving need. Willing volunteers want to help.
options.consequence: Coverage reaches 98%. Within three months, six of your most experienced volunteers burn out and leave at once. The system adjusts by pushing the next most willing group harder.
options.reflection: Optimising for a single number makes everything else invisible. Volunteer wellbeing is part of humanity — it applies to those who help as well as those helped.

options.label: Build in limits and rest
options.detail: Maximum shifts per week, mandatory rest after night shifts, and a 'no thanks' that never counts against anyone.
options.consequence: Coverage drops to 90%, and you recruit to fill the gap. Volunteer retention improves sharply, and the retired teacher comes back after a month's rest.
options.reflection: Good systems encode care. Rules that protect people from being overused are humanitarian safeguards, not inefficiencies.

options.label: Let volunteers see and shape the rules
options.detail: Publish how the roster is built and set up a volunteer panel that can change the priorities.
options.consequence: The panel asks for fairness between language groups and for weekend shifts to rotate. The system becomes slower to change but far more trusted.
options.reflection: Transparency about how decisions are made lets people challenge them. Shared rules are easier to accept than hidden ones.

steps.title: Messages that never stop
steps.narrative: The vendor proposes an AI chat assistant that sends each volunteer personalised messages, reminders and 'motivational nudges', written fresh by a large language model for every message — about 30,000 messages a month across Polish, Ukrainian and English.

options.label: Turn on personalised AI messages
options.detail: Warm, tailored messages in three languages, generated one by one.
options.consequence: Volunteers find the messages friendly at first, then strange — one receives a 'we miss you!' while in hospital. The energy report shows the messages are now the system's largest energy use, for text that said much the same each time.
options.reflection: Generating fresh text for every routine message multiplies computing for little gain. Generative AI is not free: each message has an energy and water cost.

options.label: Human-written templates in each language
options.detail: Volunteers from each language community write short message templates once. The system fills in names and times.
options.consequence: The messages sound like real people because they were written by real people. Computing needs drop to almost nothing, and volunteers enjoy writing the templates together.
options.reflection: Often the right amount of AI is less AI. Reusing human-written text is cheaper, lighter and more trustworthy.

options.label: Fewer messages, by volunteer choice
options.detail: Volunteers choose how and how often they hear from you. The default is one weekly summary.
options.consequence: Message volume drops by 80%. Some shifts fill a little more slowly, but volunteers say they feel respected rather than chased.
options.reflection: Letting people set their own boundaries reduces both pressure and footprint.

steps.title: A request from the authorities
steps.narrative: The regional authorities ask for your volunteer roster data — names, nationalities, availability — to plan their own civil-defence response. The system makes the export one click away. Many of your volunteers are Ukrainian citizens with temporary protection status.

options.label: Share the full export
options.detail: Good cooperation with the authorities helps the overall response.
options.consequence: The data is used for planning, and later for checking residence status. Volunteers learn about it from a local news report. Recruitment among Ukrainian volunteers collapses.
options.reflection: Data given for one purpose and used for another betrays trust — and can compromise the Movement's independence and neutrality in the eyes of the communities it serves.

options.label: Share only aggregated numbers
options.detail: Offer counts by skill, language and district — no names or nationalities.
options.consequence: The authorities get what they need for planning. They grumble at first, then adopt your format as a template for other organisations.
options.reflection: Purpose limitation means sharing what's needed for the stated goal and no more. Aggregates protect individuals while still supporting cooperation.

options.label: Ask volunteers to opt in
options.detail: Explain the request and let each volunteer decide whether to be listed with the authorities.
options.consequence: About half agree. The rest are grateful to have been asked. It takes three weeks — the authorities find this slow, but accept it.
options.reflection: Consent and transparency keep people in control of their own information, even when the request comes from a partner.

title: The Heat Map
tagline: AI forecasting to protect older people during a heatwave in Sicily
role: Head of Emergency Health, Red Cross regional committee in Palermo
context: Summer temperatures in Sicily now regularly pass 45°C. Last July, older people living alone died in their apartments before anyone checked on them. A European research consortium offers an AI model that combines weather forecasts, health records, phone data and satellite imagery to predict which streets and which people face the highest risk — so your volunteers know where to knock first. Running it requires a powerful computing cluster in Northern Europe.
debrief: The Heat Map captures a hard paradox: AI used to respond to climate change can itself add to the energy and resource use that drives it. Prediction can save lives, but only if it doesn't exclude the people it fails to see, doesn't take more data than needed, and is sized honestly against its own footprint.

steps.title: How big a model?
steps.narrative: The consortium's model is huge: it reprocesses European satellite imagery and climate simulations every few hours. Your information officer estimates that one summer of running it would use as much electricity as a small Sicilian village. A local university offers a simpler alternative: a statistical heat-risk index built from forecasts, building age and age data by neighbourhood.

options.label: Use the large AI model
options.detail: The most precise predictions available — at the energy cost of a village.
options.consequence: The predictions are excellent for the city centre. But the model's appetite for computing means it runs only twice a day, and its large footprint becomes a story in the Italian press: 'Red Cross fights heat with a machine that heats the planet'.
options.reflection: Climate-response tools must be judged by their own climate footprint. The most powerful model is not automatically the most humane one.

options.label: Use the simple heat-risk index
options.detail: Less precise, runs on a laptop, and explainable to any volunteer.
options.consequence: The index points to the same high-risk areas for 90% of cases. Volunteers understand why a street is red, and community leaders can correct it — which they do, adding two neighbourhoods the data missed.
options.reflection: Simple, explainable models invite participation and correction. Fit-for-purpose is often better than state-of-the-art.

options.label: Large model, but only during heat alerts
options.detail: Run the big model only when the national service issues a red alert.
options.consequence: Energy use falls by 80%. But the model starts 'cold' on alert days and takes hours to produce useful results — the first, deadliest day is the one it covers worst.
options.reflection: Limiting use is a good instinct. But compromises have to be checked against when people are actually most at risk.

steps.title: Who is invisible?
steps.narrative: The model relies on phone data and registered health records. Your volunteers point out who that misses: undocumented migrant farm workers living in informal settlements outside the city, and older people without smartphones. Neither group appears on the heat map.

options.label: Trust the map
options.detail: Volunteers are limited. Go where the data says risk is highest.
options.consequence: Visits are efficient and many lives are protected in the city. In an informal settlement near Campobello, two farm workers are hospitalised with heatstroke. No one had visited.
options.reflection: Data reflects who is counted, not who is at risk. Allocating help by data alone can quietly exclude the most vulnerable.

options.label: Reserve teams for the unmapped
options.detail: A third of volunteer capacity goes to places and groups the data can't see, guided by community contacts.
options.consequence: City coverage is slightly thinner. Settlement visits bring water, shade and early treatment to hundreds of workers the model never knew existed.
options.reflection: Impartiality means help according to need, not according to visibility. Human knowledge must correct the data's blind spots.

options.label: Collect more data on the missing
options.detail: Ask migrant workers to register their location on a phone app so the model can include them.
options.consequence: Few register — many fear immigration authorities. Those who do create a dataset that the consortium later asks to share with other partners.
options.reflection: Making invisible people visible to a system can expose them to new risks. Sometimes the safer answer is to work around the data, not to fill it.

steps.title: Cooling the servers
steps.narrative: The consortium proposes to install a local computing cluster in Palermo to make predictions faster. In a heatwave, the servers themselves would need constant air-conditioning — drawing power from the same strained grid that keeps older people's fans running. During last year's heatwave, parts of the city lost power.

options.label: Install the local cluster
options.detail: Faster predictions, local control.
options.consequence: On the hottest day the grid operator asks for voluntary cuts. Your servers keep running — and keep cooling — while two neighbourhoods have rolling blackouts.
options.reflection: AI infrastructure competes with people for energy and water, sometimes exactly when both are scarcest. That competition is a humanitarian question.

options.label: Keep it light and solar-powered
options.detail: Run the simple index on laptops at the operations centre, powered by rooftop solar with battery backup.
options.consequence: The system runs even during the blackout. The batteries also keep the operations centre's phones and fridges for medicines working.
options.reflection: Resilient, low-energy design protects operations when infrastructure fails — which is when crisis tools matter most.

options.label: Compute in Northern Europe, on renewables
options.detail: Leave the heavy computing in a hydro-powered data centre in Norway or Sweden.
options.consequence: The local grid is spared, and the electricity is renewable. But connectivity during the heatwave is unreliable, and you depend on a link you don't control when it matters most.
options.reflection: Moving computing to clean energy reduces emissions but not dependency. Weigh both the footprint and who keeps control in a crisis.

steps.title: Knocking on the door
steps.narrative: On alert days, the system gives each volunteer a list of addresses ranked by predicted risk. A volunteer asks: 'What do I say when an old man asks why we chose him?' Another reports that some residents feel labelled as 'about to die'.

options.label: Don't explain — just help
options.detail: The model is too complex to explain at the doorstep.
options.consequence: Most people accept the visit. Some don't open the door. A rumour spreads that the Red Cross has secret lists from the hospital.
options.reflection: When people don't know why they've been selected, suspicion fills the gap. Opacity erodes the trust that humanitarian work depends on.

options.label: Explain plainly and offer a way out
options.detail: A simple script: 'This street is hot and has many older residents. Would you like us to check in during the heatwave?' People can say no and be removed.
options.consequence: Almost everyone says yes. A few opt out, and their choice is respected. Neighbours start telling volunteers about other people living alone.
options.reflection: Being clear about why help is offered — and accepting a 'no' — respects dignity and turns a prediction into a relationship.

options.label: Let neighbourhoods own the list
options.detail: Share the area-level heat map with parish groups and neighbourhood associations, who decide whom to check on.
options.consequence: Coverage becomes uneven — strong in organised neighbourhoods, weak elsewhere. But where it works, the checking continues all summer, with no model needed.
options.reflection: Putting communities in charge builds lasting capacity, but you still need to watch for those without a strong community around them.
